chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad ibn Ali, from Musa ibn Sa'dan, from Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

He said: There is no oath in anger, nor in cutting off kinship, nor in compulsion, nor in coercion. I said: May Allah improve you, so what is the difference between coercion and compulsion? He said: Compulsion is from the Sultan (ruling authority), and coercion happens from the wife, the mother, and the father, and that is not [considered valid/obligatory].
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between compulsion and coercion in Shia jurisprudence regarding oaths?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between 'ijbar' (compulsion by the ruling authority) and 'ikrah' (coercion by family members), ruling that oaths taken under these pressures or in anger are not binding. It highlights the Shia legal principle that external force negates the voluntary intent required for an oath to be valid, ensuring fairness in personal and social obligations.
